grammar.explanation: 이다 links a noun to the subject ("A is B") and attaches directly to the noun. In casual speech use ~이야 after a consonant and ~야 after a vowel; in polite speech ~이에요 after a consonant and ~예요 after a vowel; formally ~입니다 for both. The negative 아니다 becomes 아니야, 아니에요 and 아닙니다, with the noun usually marked by 이/가.

examples.en: I am an office worker.
This meat is beef.
This is a theater.
That is not my passport.

grammar.explanation: To say something "was" a noun, add 었 to the stem 이, giving ~이었어(요), ~이었다 or ~이었습니다. After a noun ending in a vowel, 이었 usually shrinks to 였. 아니다 follows the normal rule and becomes 아니었어요.

examples.en: That place was a factory.
My friend was a doctor.
Yesterday was P.E. class.
That person was not a student.

grammar.explanation: The everyday way to talk about the future is to add ~ㄹ (after a vowel) or ~을 (after a consonant) to a verb or adjective stem, follow it with 것 ("thing"), and finish with 이다. In speech 것이에요 is shortened to 거예요 (casual 거야). This form is more common than ~겠~ for plain future statements.

examples.en: I will visit my friend tomorrow.
Class will start at nine.
We will eat pork in the evening.
I will become a teacher in the future.

grammar.explanation: Adding ~ㄹ/을 to a verb or adjective stem turns it into a describing word for something that will happen, so it must be followed by a noun. This is exactly how 할 것 works: 할 describes the noun 것. It parallels ~ㄴ/은 on adjectives (좋은 사람).

examples.en: There is no food to eat tomorrow.
I have a lot of work to do.
The movie we will watch today is fun.

grammar.point: Two number systems (Sino-Korean and pure Korean)
grammar.explanation: Korean has Chinese-derived numbers (일, 이, 삼...) and native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋...). Sino-Korean numbers are used for money, phone numbers, math, measurements, minutes and most dates; pure Korean numbers are used for counting things, people and actions and for the hour. Big numbers are built by stacking units, and 만 (10,000) is its own unit. Zero is 영 for scores and temperature, and 공 for phone numbers.

examples.en: This book is 10,000 won.
My phone number is 010-555-1234.

examples.ko: 우리 팀이 이 대 영으로 이겼어요.
examples.en: Our team won two to zero.
I have two younger siblings.

grammar.explanation: When counting, put the noun first and then a pure Korean number plus a counter word: noun + number + counter. 개 is the general counter for things, 명 for people, 대 for vehicles and 잔 for cups or glasses. Before a counter, 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 change to 한/두/세/네/스무, and the written number is separated from the counter by a space.

examples.en: I bought three pieces of bread.
There are five students in the classroom.
Two coffees, please.

examples.ko: 우리 회사에 차가 네 대 있어요.
examples.en: Our company has four cars.

grammar.explanation: A pure Korean number + 번 tells how many times an action happens. The combination works like an adverb, so it normally takes no particle and sits before the verb.

examples.en: I went to Korea three times.

examples.ko: 저는 오늘 고기를 두 번 먹었어요.
examples.en: I ate meat twice today.
I watched that movie once.

grammar.point: Telling time (시 and 분) and age (살)
grammar.explanation: For clock time, the hour uses pure Korean numbers + 시 and the minutes use Sino-Korean numbers + 분. Age is usually given with pure Korean numbers + 살. With numerals, the space before the counter is often dropped (3시 20분).

examples.en: It is 3:20 now.
Class starts at nine o'clock.
I am twenty-two years old.
My younger sibling is ten years old.

grammar.point: Ordinals with 번째, plus 처음 and 마지막
grammar.explanation: Adding 번째 after a pure Korean number makes an ordinal (second, third...), but "first" is 첫 번째. 처음 means the first time or the beginning, and 마지막 means last in a sequence (not "last" meaning previous).

examples.en: This is my second class.
I was the first person.
I rode the subway for the first time.
Today is the last day.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: 동안, Seconds, Minutes, Hours, Days, Weeks, Months, Years

grammar.explanation: Place 동안 right after a length of time to say how long something lasts, like English "for". No extra particle is needed after 동안. Use whichever number system the time word requires.

examples.en: I drove for two hours.
He ran for ten minutes.

examples.ko: 우리는 삼 일 동안 서울에 있었어요.
examples.en: We were in Seoul for three days.

examples.ko: 저는 일 년 동안 한국어를 공부했어요.
examples.en: I studied Korean for one year.

grammar.point: Counting units of time (초, 분, 시간, 일, 주, 달/개월, 년)
grammar.explanation: Seconds (초), minutes (분), days (일), weeks (주), months with 개월, and years (년) take Sino-Korean numbers. Hours counted as a duration use 시간 with pure Korean numbers (시 is only for clock time), and months counted with 달 also use pure Korean numbers.

examples.en: I cooked for three hours.

examples.ko: 저는 한국에서 육 개월 동안 살았어요.
examples.en: I lived in Korea for six months.

examples.ko: 저는 한국에서 여섯 달 동안 살았어요.
examples.en: I lived in Korea for six months.

examples.ko: 그 수업은 이 주 동안 해요.
examples.en: That class runs for two weeks.

grammar.point: 지난 / 이번 / 다음 and 작년 / 올해 / 내년
grammar.explanation: 지난 (previous), 이번 (this) and 다음 (next) go before 주 and 달 to mean last/this/next week or month, and before 번 for last/this/next time. They cannot be used with 년; instead use 작년 (last year), 올해 (this year) and 내년 (next year). 마지막 means final, not previous.

examples.en: I went to the theater last week.
I will visit my grandmother next month.
I have plans this week.
I will go to Korea next year.

grammar.explanation: 일 counts days with Sino-Korean numbers and also gives dates, written month then day (5월 5일). 날 means "day" as a noun but is not used for counting. For short spans there are special words: 하루 (one day), 이틀 (two days), 사흘 (three days).

examples.en: My birthday is May 5th.
I was sick for two days.
That day was really cold.
I rested at home for a day.

grammar.explanation: Attaching ~에 to a unit of time expresses frequency within that unit, like English "per" or "a". Put the time + 에 first, then the amount (often with 번 or another counter).

examples.en: I run twice a week.

examples.ko: 저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔 마셔요.
examples.en: I drink three cups of coffee a day.

examples.ko: 저는 한 달에 책을 한 권 읽어요.
examples.en: I read one book a month.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Korean Particles 들, 만, 에서, 부터, 까지, (으)로

vocab.en: to get off, to come down

grammar.explanation: Korean speakers usually leave out the subject or topic, especially 저/나, when it is clear from context. Sentences without 저는 are complete and sound more natural in conversation.

examples.en: (I) went to the theater yesterday.
What are (you) doing now?
(I) will meet a friend tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: ~들 attached to a noun (usually people or animals) marks it as plural, but Korean often leaves plurals unmarked when the meaning is clear. 몇 + counter asks "how many", and in a statement it means "a few".

examples.en: The students are playing soccer in the park.
My friends came to our house.
How many apples did you buy?
A few people were late.

grammar.explanation: ~만 attaches to a noun to mean "only" or "just". It can replace 이/가 or 을/를, or stack on top of other particles such as 에서만.

examples.en: I only drank water.
Only that student came.
I only study at home.

grammar.explanation: Besides marking where an action happens, ~에서 marks the starting point or origin of movement, meaning "from". It is often used with verbs like 오다 and 출발하다.

examples.en: I came from Canada.
The train departed from Seoul.
That person came out of the room.

grammar.explanation: ~부터 marks a starting time or point and ~까지 marks the end point, like "from ... to/until". For places, ~에서 is usually paired with ~까지 instead of ~부터.

examples.ko: 저는 아홉 시부터 다섯 시까지 일해요.
examples.en: I work from nine to five.
I have class from Monday to Friday.
I drove from Seoul to Busan.
I will study hard starting tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: ~(으)로 (~로 after a vowel or ㄹ, ~으로 after other consonants) shows direction toward a place, the tool or method used, or what something changes into. It often translates as "to/toward", "by" or "with".

examples.en: I go to work by subway.
I wrote the sentence with a pencil.
Please go to the left.
I changed my car for a new one.

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Korean Particles: and, with, to, from, for, about

grammar.explanation: To join two nouns with "and", attach 와 (after a vowel) or 과 (after a consonant), 하고, or 랑/이랑 to the first noun. 와/과 sounds more formal or written, 하고 is neutral, and (이)랑 is casual.

examples.en: I bought bread and milk.
Mom and Dad are at home.
I drank green tea and coffee.

grammar.explanation: The same particles also mean "with" when attached to a person you do something with. 같이 ("together") is often added after the particle to make the meaning clear.

examples.en: I listened to music with my friend.
I watched a movie with my younger sibling.
I had lunch with the teacher.
I will marry that person.

grammar.explanation: When giving, saying or sending something to a person or animal, attach 에게 (neutral/written) or 한테 (spoken). 께 is the honorific version for respected people. Use 에, not these, for places.

examples.en: I sent a text to my friend.
I gave bread to my younger sibling.
I gave flowers to my grandmother.

grammar.explanation: To show that something came from a person, add 에게서 or the more spoken 한테서. (으)로부터 also means "from" and sounds formal, often used for organizations or in writing.

examples.en: I received a present from my friend.
I got a book from the teacher.
I received a letter from the government.

grammar.explanation: Attach 을/를 위해 or 을/를 위해서 to a noun to say you do something for the benefit of that person or thing. It comes before the action it explains.

examples.en: I work for my family.
We prepared dinner for Mom.
I run every day for my health.

grammar.explanation: Attach 에 대해 or 에 대해서 to a noun to mean "about" or "regarding" that topic. It is common with verbs of speaking, knowing and thinking.

examples.en: We talked about Korean music.
I didn't know about that fact.
The teacher taught about Korean history.

vocab.en: to put out, to produce (e.g. 화를 내다 = to get angry)

grammar.explanation: Many 하다 verbs become passive by swapping 하다 for 되다, so the subject receives the action instead of doing it. Because the result is passive, the noun takes 이/가 rather than 을/를.

examples.en: The class started (was started).
Tax is included in the price.
That machine was replaced with a new one.

grammar.explanation: Some 하다 verbs, especially ones describing how people treat someone, become passive with 받다 ("to receive"). 존경받다 means "to be respected" and 사랑받다 "to be loved". The person doing the action is marked with 에게/한테.

examples.en: That teacher is respected by students.
That actor is loved by many people.
I was praised by the teacher.

grammar.explanation: Many non-하다 verbs have a passive form made by inserting 이, 히, 리 or 기 into the stem, such as 열다 → 열리다, 닫다 → 닫히다, 잠그다 → 잠기다 and 놓다 → 놓이다. There is no rule for which suffix a verb takes, so learn each one as vocabulary.

examples.en: The door opened (was opened).
The window was closed.
That room was locked.
The box was placed on the desk.

grammar.explanation: Words ending in 내다 describe causing something to happen, while the matching 나다 form describes it happening by itself: 고장내다 means "to break", 고장나다 "to be broken". 나다 also appears in fixed phrases like 화나다, 짜증나다 and 냄새가 나다.

examples.en: I broke the computer.
The computer is broken.
I got angry today.
A nice smell is coming from the kitchen.

grammar.explanation: Verbs without a special passive form can usually become passive by adding ~아/어지다 to the stem, so 켜다 → 켜지다 and 끄다 → 꺼지다. The thing affected becomes the subject with 이/가.

examples.en: The light came on.
The TV suddenly turned off.
The cup broke.

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Miscellaneous Words and Grammar: 들다, Korean Homonyms, Being Sick, Different/Similar/Same

vocab.en: to lift, to carry, to hold
to be caught, to be stuck
to be noisy, to be loud

grammar.explanation: Feeling adjectives like 좋다 and 싫다 describe something as good or disliked, while adding ~아/어하다 to the stem turns them into action verbs: 좋아하다 "to like", 싫어하다 "to dislike". The verb version takes an object with 을/를 and is the natural way to describe what another person feels.

examples.en: I like meat.
My younger sibling dislikes rain.
That child is afraid of dogs.

grammar.explanation: An adjective can never act on an object, so a sentence like "I like X" built with an adjective marks X with 이/가, not 을/를. The pattern is topic (저는) + thing with 이/가 + adjective. It also works with adjectives such as 그립다 and 자랑스럽다.

examples.en: I like that song.
I don't like cats.
I am proud of you.
I miss Korean food.

grammar.explanation: 들다 has several unrelated meanings: to lift or hold something, to enter or go into, to cost (money or effort), and in 마음에 들다, to be to one's liking. Work out which meaning applies from the surrounding words.

examples.en: I lifted a heavy box.
I like this hat.
Studying abroad costs a lot of money.

grammar.explanation: Korean often joins two verbs with ~아/어 to make one compound verb, like 돌다 + 가다 → 돌아가다 (to go back) or 가지다 + 오다 → 가져오다 (to bring). The first verb shows how the action is done and the second, often 가다 or 오다, shows the direction.

examples.en: I went back home early.
My friend brought a book.
I looked back.
Please give that book back.

grammar.explanation: To compare two things, use the noun + 와/과 (or 하고, 랑) + 다르다 (different), 비슷하다 (similar) or 같다 (same). 똑같다 stresses "exactly the same", and 다른 + noun means "another, a different" one.

examples.en: Korean food is different from Japanese food.
My older brother is similar to my father.
These two bags are exactly the same.
My hobby is the same as my friend's hobby.

grammar.point: Homonyms such as 걸리다 and 배
grammar.explanation: Some Korean words have several unrelated meanings that you tell apart by context. 걸리다 can mean to hang, to be caught, to catch an illness, or to take an amount of time, and 배 can mean pear, stomach or boat.

examples.en: It takes ten minutes to get to school.
I caught a cold.
A picture was hung on the wall.
I ate a pear.

grammar.explanation: Common phrases are body part + 이/가 아프다 for pain, illness + 에 걸리다 for catching a cold or the flu, 열이 나다 for running a fever, and 기침을 하다 for coughing.

examples.en: My throat hurts.
I caught the flu.
My son had a fever.
I coughed a lot at night.

vocab.en: to untie, to unfasten, to loosen
to be close to, to be near

grammar.explanation: Adding ~적 to many Sino-Korean nouns makes an "-ic/-al" form: 역사 → 역사적 (historical). Use ~적인 before a noun to describe it, ~적으로 as an adverb ("-ically"), and ~적이다 to end a sentence like an adjective.

examples.en: That is a historic place.
This car is really economical.
We explained that problem scientifically.
Personally, I like that movie.

grammar.explanation: ~스럽다 attaches to certain nouns to make an adjective meaning "having that quality" or "giving that feeling", such as 사랑 → 사랑스럽다 (lovely) and 자연 → 자연스럽다 (natural). It conjugates like other ㅂ-irregular adjectives: 스러워요, 스러운.

examples.en: That child is really lovely.
The result was disappointing.
His Korean is very natural.
I am satisfied with this result.

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Connecting Particle ~고 and ~고 싶다 "I want to"

grammar.explanation: Attach ~고 to a verb or adjective stem (or ~이고 after a noun) to link two clauses, meaning "and" or "and then". Tense and politeness go only on the final verb. With 은/는 on both subjects, ~고 can set two contrasting facts side by side.

examples.en: I ate and then went to school.
The weather is warm and the wind is cool.

examples.ko: 이 산은 높고 저 산은 낮아요.
examples.en: This mountain is high and that one is low.
That person is rich and kind.

grammar.explanation: ~아/어서 also connects one action to the next, but it implies the first action leads into the second. With 가다 and 오다 you must use 가서/와서 when you go somewhere and then do something there. The verb before ~아/어서 never takes past tense.

examples.en: I went to the market and bought fruit.
My friend came to our house and rested.
I opened the door and went outside.

grammar.explanation: Position verbs like 앉다, 서다 and 눕다 take ~아/어서 rather than ~고 when the second action happens while in that position. Using ~고 would suggest you sat, got up, and then did something else.

examples.en: I sat on the sofa and watched TV.
We stood in line and waited.
I lay on the bed and listened to music.

grammar.explanation: Add ~고 싶다 to a verb stem to say you want to do something; conjugate 싶다 for tense and politeness (싶어요, 싶었어요). With 되다 it means "want to become". 보고 싶다 is also how you say you miss a person.

examples.en: I want to go to the sea.
I want to rest today.
I wanted to become a chef.
I miss my mom so much.

grammar.explanation: ~은/는 marks the topic and often carries a comparing or contrasting feel ("as for X..."), while ~이/가 simply identifies the subject and puts the focus on it. When two things are contrasted, both usually take 은/는.

examples.en: The weather is nice.
Today, the weather is nice.
Grammar is hard, but vocabulary is easy.
Who came?
